title: Binary search
subject: Algorithms
prompt: Explain how binary search finds a value in a list. Say why the list must be sorted, how the search range changes at each step, when the search stops, and how fast it is.

points.statement: The list must be sorted, because each comparison relies on order to rule out half the list.
points.hint: Say why sorting is required, not only that it is.

points.statement: Each step compares the target with the middle element of the current range.
points.hint: Name the middle element as the thing being compared.

points.statement: The range shrinks by moving the low or high bound past the middle, discarding the half that cannot hold the target.
points.hint: Describe how the low and high bounds move.

points.statement: The search stops when the target is found, or when the range is empty (low passes high) and it reports not found.
points.hint: Explain both ways the search can end.

points.statement: It runs in O(log n) time because the range halves at every step.
points.hint: Give the time complexity and the reason for it.

points.statement: It is much faster than linear search on large lists, which checks every element.

trap.false_claim: Binary search also works on an unsorted list, as long as the list is long enough.
trap.truth: Order is what lets one comparison rule out half the list. On an unsorted list, binary search can miss the target entirely.

probe.kp1: You said the list has to be sorted. What exactly goes wrong if it isn't?
probe.kp2: Which element does binary search compare the target with first, and why that one?
probe.kp3: After comparing with the middle, how do low and high change? Walk me through one step.
probe.kp4: How does the search know it should stop when the value isn't in the list?
probe.kp5: How many steps does binary search need for a list of about a million items?
probe.kp6: When would you still choose linear search over binary search?

follow_ups.what_if: What happens if the value you are looking for appears several times in the list?
